title: Handling Underperformance
description: Addressing senior leader underperformance with clarity, fairness, documentation, compassion, and decisiveness.

competency.name: Handling Underperformance
competency.definition: Distinguishes skill gaps, role mismatch, and motivation problems, then acts fairly and decisively.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior leaders damage organizations when they tolerate unclear expectations or avoid difficult people decisions.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you had to address underperformance in a senior leader.
variants: Describe a time when you waited too long to make a people decision.
Tell me about a time a well-liked leader was not scaling with the role.
interviewerIntent: Can the candidate be fair and direct?
Do they distinguish role mismatch from character judgment?
Can they act decisively without losing compassion?

scenario.signatureExample: An engineering director realizes one manager is well-liked but unable to scale as the organization grows.
context: The manager has strong trust with engineers but weak planning and delegation.
Team delivery depends too much on personal heroics.
Peers are frustrated by missed commitments but reluctant to criticize the person.
constraints: The leader deserves clear expectations and support.
The business cannot keep absorbing delivery misses.
The decision will signal how the organization handles performance.

storyAnatomy.situation: A respected manager was struggling with scale, creating repeated delivery and delegation problems.
storyAnatomy.task: Address the performance gap clearly and fairly while protecting the team and business outcomes.
action: Created a time-bound improvement plan with coaching and reduced ambiguity.
Eventually moved the person into a better-fitting role when improvement was insufficient.
result: The team gained clearer planning and ownership.
The individual was treated respectfully and placed where they could succeed.
The organization saw that **performance expectations** were real and humane.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The hard lesson was that compassion without clarity prolongs stress for everyone involved.
systemChange: Role-fit review before expanding management scope.

exampleStories.title: Beloved Manager Not Scaling
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you had to address underperformance in a senior leader.
exampleStories.situation: A manager was trusted and well-liked but could not delegate, plan across teams, or develop leads as the organization scaled.
strongAnswerSketch: Describe observable gaps rather than labeling the person.
Clarify expectations and create a time-bound **coaching plan**.
Measure progress through delegation, planning quality, and team ownership.
Move the person into a better-fitting role when the gap remained.
whyItWorks: Protects the team from prolonged ambiguity.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I gave them feedback several times, but eventually it was clear they were not a fit and we had to move on.
followUpAngles: What exact expectation did they miss?
How long did you give the **coaching plan**?

exampleStories.title: Senior IC In A Lead Role Mismatch
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when you waited too long to make a people decision.
exampleStories.situation: A senior IC was made a team lead because of technical depth, but they avoided feedback conversations and became a bottleneck for decisions.
strongAnswerSketch: Acknowledge the leadership design mistake instead of blaming the person.
Clarify whether the issue is skill gap, motivation, or role mismatch.
Offer coaching and an alternate senior IC path.
Change **promotion criteria** for future lead assignments.
whyItWorks: Creates a fairer leadership selection mechanism.
exampleStories.weakVersion: The person was not leadership material, so I replaced them with someone more people-oriented.
followUpAngles: How did you preserve the person dignity?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows clear expectations, evidence, coaching, documentation, and timely action.
moves: Describes observable performance gaps rather than labels.
Gives the person a fair chance with explicit expectations.
Acts when the situation does not improve.
Reflects on timing and system improvements.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate either avoids the issue or describes a cold termination without coaching, documentation, or learning.
redFlags: Cannot name the expectation the person failed to meet.
Confuses being liked with being effective.
Delegates the hard conversation to HR or another leader.
Lets the situation continue until team trust is damaged.

followUps.question: What expectations did you make explicit?
What support did you provide before making a final decision?
Did you act too early, too late, or at the right time?
How did you manage the impact on the team?

signals.name: Clarity
signals.strong: Names expectations, gaps, support, and **decision criteria**.

signals.name: Fairness
signals.strong: Provides support and evidence before making a decision.
signals.weak: Surprises the person or skips feedback.

signals.name: Decisiveness
signals.strong: Acts when evidence shows the role is not working.

rubric.expected: Handles team-level performance with clear feedback and documentation.
Addresses manager underperformance across teams while protecting delivery and trust.
Makes senior leadership changes with fairness, speed, and organizational clarity.
Handles executive-level role fit and succession implications with company-level judgment.

prompts.label: What performance gap was visible and consequential?
What decision or support process did you own?
How did you clarify, coach, document, and decide?
What changed for the person, team, and organization?
What would you change about your timing or approach?

relatedScenarios: A senior IC in a leadership role blocks delegation.
A manager is culturally beloved but delivery-poor.
A director cannot scale from team execution to organizational leadership.
